scripts.radio:
Jambo Kenya, welcome back to Kenya on Record. I am your host, and today we must have a serious conversation about our children's future.

For years, we have heard grand promises about digital learning, classroom tablets, and preparing our youth for the modern global economy. But here is the hard reality: only twenty percent of primary and secondary schools in Kenya currently have working internet connectivity. That means eight out of ten schools are completely offline.

Millions of students in public schools are being left behind while their peers in elite private institutions navigate the digital world with ease. How do we expect our children to compete when they have never touched a connected computer? Where did the billions allocated for school ICT infrastructure and electrification actually go?

Connectivity is no longer a luxury; it is a basic right in modern education. As parents and taxpayers, we must demand transparency. Ask your local MP today: what is the status of internet connectivity in your constituency’s public schools?

Kwa muhtasari wa Kiswahili:
Ni asilimia ishirini tu ya shule zote nchini Kenya zilizo na mtandao wa intaneti. Hii inaanisha wanafunzi wengi sana wanapitwa na elimu ya kidijitali. Ni wakati wa kuwawajibisha viongozi wetu na kuuliza jinsi pesa za serikali za miundombinu ya shule zilivyotumika.

Keep following Kenya on Record. Stay informed, stay accountable.
scripts.voice_note:
Habari zenu, members of Kenya on Record. Quick check-in today on a story that affects almost every family in this country.

Did you know that only 20% of Kenyan schools have internet connectivity? That means 80% of our children are attending schools with zero access to digital learning tools.

We were promised a digital revolution in education. Billions of taxpayers' shillings have been budgeted over the years for school tech. Yet, millions of kids are finishing school without basic digital skills simply because their school lacks internet.

This isn't just a statistic; it’s about equal opportunity. A child in a rural public school deserves the same access to information as any other child. Share this message, talk to your local school board, and ask your CDF managers where the tech budget goes. Let's keep them accountable.
